analysis.one_liner: Bans a cancer-linked pesticide residue (daminozide, sold as Alar) from food within 90 days.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban daminozide residues in food died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Daminozide, a pesticide sprayed on apples and other crops, leaves a residue called UDMH that the EPA had classified as a potent carcinogen. The bill would end the legal limit (tolerance) allowing daminozide residue in food within 90 days, citing children's higher fruit consumption and developing bodies. It never got a hearing or vote: after introduction, it was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its health subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, children and all consumers of apples and other treated produce, who would no longer eat UDMH residue in their food.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and consumers of treated produce

how_it_helps.text: Terminates the legal tolerance for daminozide in food no later than 90 days after enactment, eliminating UDMH residues from treated produce.
The bill's stated findings cite EPA's conclusion that UDMH is a potent human carcinogen and argue the risk to children, who eat proportionately more fruits and vegetables, is unacceptably high.
The bill faults EPA for having authority to prohibit daminozide on food and failing to use it, aiming to force removal faster than the agency's own process.
The legislation directs that use of daminozide on food be immediately prohibited in order to protect children's health.

analysis.who_pays: The maker of daminozide, which would lose sales of the pesticide, and growers who used it on apples and other crops, which would need to switch to other pest-control methods or absorb any yield or shelf-life losses.

drawbacks.text: An abrupt 90-day ban would give growers little time to adjust, forcing them to find alternatives for a pesticide that helped apples stay red and firm through shipping and storage.

The bill overrides the EPA's ongoing tolerance-setting process by statute; some would argue scientific risk assessment belongs with the expert agency rather than a legislative deadline set on a single chemical.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward: removing a suspected carcinogen from food children eat heavily versus short-term costs to growers and the pesticide's maker. The main design weakness is the rigid 90-day deadline, which addresses grower transition only through the short wind-down period. The bigger story is that none of this was tested — the bill drew no cosponsors and never reached a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerry Sikorski introduced the bill on March 20, 1989, with no cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On April 3, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, where action ended.
No further action was taken during the 101st Congress, which ended January 3, 1991, so the bill never reached the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The maker of daminozide and growers who used it benefited, since the legal tolerance for the residue in food remained in place; EPA's slower regulatory process continued instead of the immediate statutory ban.

for.name: Rep. Gerry Sikorski
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate the daminozide tolerance and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never acted on it; its Subcommittee on Health and the Environment held it from April 1989 until the Congress ended without a hearing or vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member cosponsored, so the partisan shape of support and opposition never became visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have ended legal tolerance for daminozide residue in food within 90 days, cutting off the product's food uses. Because the bill died, sales and the legal residue limit continued.

industries.industry: Apple and produce growers using daminozide
industries.note: Growers would have had to stop spraying the chemical and find alternatives within 90 days. The bill's failure let them keep using it on apples and other crops.
